newsitem.title: GERMANY: ALPINE SKIING-SAFETY PROBE AFTER NEAR-MISS ON WORLD CUP SLOPE.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-SAFETY PROBE AFTER NEAR-MISS ON WORLD CUP SLOPE.

text.p: The question of safety on one of the most dangerous mountains in Alpine skiing was thrown into the spotlight again on Saturday when a spectator nearly caused a serious accident during a men's World Cup downhill.

Italian racer Pietro Vitalini was forced to stop in the middle of his high-speed run to avoid a spectator who had lost his balance on the icy hill at Garmisch-Partenkirchen and slid across the piste in front of him.

Vitalini, who later raced again and managed to finish second, was shocked by the incident on the same German mountain where former world champion Ulrike Maier was killed in a women's race three years ago.
"I still felt a bit shaky an hour after the race," he said. "The problem was not having to start again but that I was really lucky that I did not have a bad accident when the guy slid.
"It was already difficult to master my line at that point because it was fast. I was very lucky to avoid a crash at that point....We both could have been in serious trouble."
Garmisch organisers, who were involved in a long-running law suit about the Maier crash, started an investigation into the incident.
It was not immediately clear how the man, who was not wearing skis, managed to stray on to the piste with the racers hurtling down at speeds of more than 100 kph.

"We are going to go into this matter. It is very embarrassing," chief organiser Hubert Ostler said. "A great deal has been done about safety since the Maier crash. The man seems to have disappeared but someone must have seen him."
At last year's world championships in Spain, a skier and an official ended up in hospital after a spectacular collision on the piste during training.
Garmisch is one of the most challenging courses on the World Cup circuit and has witnessed many crashes over the years.
France's downhill World Cup leader Luc Alphand, who won Saturday's race, said he could not believe what had happened.
"When I first heard about it I didn't believe it," he said. "These accidents are always stupid. We have enough obstacles skiing without putting any more there."
